title: Marine Pollution, Oil Spills and Ocean Acidification

cards.b:
Oceans absorb heat, carbon and waste. Prelims asks about spills, conventions (MARPOL, London), acidification and dead zones. Mains asks about the Indian coast and the Blue Economy.

It also links to coral reefs, fisheries and climate.

Expect a one-line match: spill name with place, or convention with subject.

About 80 percent of marine pollution comes from land: sewage, plastics, fertiliser run-off, industrial waste. The rest comes from ships (oil, garbage, ballast water) and accidents. Plastic is now found from the surface to the deep sea, and microplastics enter food chains.

Ocean gyres collect floating debris. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch lies between Hawaii and California.

• Exxon Valdez (1989): Alaska; one of the best-known tanker spills.
  • Deepwater Horizon (2010): Gulf of Mexico; the largest marine oil spill in history by volume.
  • MV Wakashio (2020): Mauritius, ran aground on a coral reef.
  • Ennore, Chennai (January 2017): two ships collided and oil reached the beach.
  • X-Press Pearl (2021): Sri Lanka; plastic pellets and chemicals.

Oil coats birds and fur, blocks light and harms fish eggs.

Spill response uses booms (floating barriers), skimmers, dispersants and in-situ burning. Bioremediation uses oil-eating bacteria. The Indian Coast Guard is the national response agency under the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (1996).

Dispersants break oil into droplets but can also be toxic. Prevention is better: double-hulled tankers, safe routes and strict inspection.

• MARPOL 73/78 (IMO): prevents pollution from ships. Six Annexes: oil, noxious liquids, harmful packaged goods, sewage, garbage, air pollution.
  • London Convention (1972) and its Protocol: dumping of wastes at sea.
  • UNCLOS (1982): the law of the sea; EEZ of 200 nautical miles.
  • Ballast Water Convention (2004) controls invasive species carried by ships.
  • OPRC 1990: preparedness against oil pollution.

India is a party to MARPOL and UNCLOS.

The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO2. The gas reacts with water to form carbonic acid and lowers pH. Since the industrial era surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 units (from about 8.2 to 8.1), around 30 percent more acidic.

Acidification makes it harder for corals, shellfish and pteropods to build calcium carbonate shells. It joins warming and deoxygenation as threats. Coral bleaching is caused by warmth, not acid, but reefs face both.

Fertiliser run-off feeds algae. When they die, bacteria use oxygen, and dead zones form. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone, fed by the Mississippi River, is a famous example. Red tides (harmful algal blooms) are another sign.

India: the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal have low-oxygen layers, and blooms have affected Kerala and Odisha coasts.

India has about 11,098 km of coastline including islands (the 2023 figure; earlier 7,516 km). The Coastal Regulation Zone rules limit building near the coast. Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar (2022) was a coastal cleanup drive. India's Blue Economy policy and the Deep Ocean Mission (2021) raise both use and risk. The National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR) works on coastal health.

• 80 percent of marine pollution comes from land.
  • MARPOL 73/78: ship pollution.
  • London Convention: dumping at sea.
  • Ocean acidification: pH down by about 0.1.
  • ICG: lead for oil spills.

Also hold the numbers: 80 percent from land, pH down by 0.1, EEZ 200 nautical miles, ICG plan 1996.

Prelims-style: "Which convention deals with pollution from ships?" (MARPOL). "Ocean acidification affects which organisms?" (corals, molluscs).

Mains-style: "Discuss the causes and consequences of marine pollution. What steps can India take?" Structure: land and sea sources; spills; acidification; legal framework; Indian measures; way forward.

Close with one Indian step, such as the Deep Ocean Mission or Swachh Sagar, Surakshit Sagar.
